questions.prompt: A software pattern is best described as:

options.text: A reusable solution to a known problem in a well-defined context
A finished library you can import

questions.explanation: A pattern is a reusable solution to a known problem within a well-defined context, defined by context, problem (forces), and solution.

questions.prompt: In the GoF classification, which category does the Singleton pattern belong to?
questions.explanation: Singleton is a creational pattern, alongside Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, and Factory Method.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are GoF structural patterns?
questions.explanation: Adapter, Decorator, and Facade are structural patterns; Observer is behavioral.

questions.prompt: Which pattern embeds each behavioral variation inside an object passed as a parameter to an algorithm?
questions.explanation: Strategy embeds each variation in a strategy object implementing a common interface, passed to the algorithm (e.g. java.util.Comparator).

questions.prompt: The Template Method pattern defines the stable core of an algorithm and lets subclasses provide variations at specific points via abstract primitive operations.
questions.explanation: Template Method keeps a stable algorithm core that invokes abstract primitive operations overridden by subclasses (e.g. the Sorter/StringSorter example).

questions.prompt: Which Proxy variant creates expensive objects only on demand?
questions.explanation: A virtual proxy creates expensive objects on demand (e.g. slow-loading resources); a remote proxy is a local representative for an object in another address space.

questions.prompt: In the MVC pattern, which part should remain as separate as possible from the user interface?
questions.explanation: Application logic (the Model) must remain as separate as possible from the user interface (View = layout, Controller = events).

questions.prompt: Inheritance and composition are both ways to achieve reuse, but composition delegates requests to an included object.
questions.explanation: With inheritance the reusing class inherits methods directly; with composition it holds an included object and delegates client requests to it.

questions.prompt: Which type of pattern expresses a fundamental structural organization schema for entire software systems?
questions.explanation: Architectural patterns address system-wide structures; design patterns refine components; idioms are language-specific low-level patterns.

questions.prompt: Which pattern lets a class with an unexpected interface be integrated without modifying its source?
questions.explanation: Adapter integrates a provider class whose interface is not the one expected, without modifying it; it is the only structural pattern where inheritance plays the key role.

questions.prompt: Which pattern represents part-whole hierarchies so clients treat individual and composed objects uniformly?
questions.explanation: Composite represents part-whole hierarchies (e.g. Java Swing JPanel containment) so clients can treat individual and composite objects the same way.

questions.prompt: The Decorator pattern adds responsibilities to individual objects dynamically without an explosion of subclasses.
questions.explanation: Decorator extends an object's behaviour dynamically without subclass explosion; Java's JScrollPane and BufferedReader are examples.

questions.prompt: Which pattern provides an object to traverse a collection without exposing its internal storage?
questions.explanation: Iterator provides an iterator object attached to the collection, allowing multiple concurrent iterations without exposing internal storage (java.util.Iterator).

questions.prompt: Which pattern supports very large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently by sharing intrinsic state?
questions.explanation: Flyweight shares common (intrinsic) state across many fine-grained objects to save memory; Java's Integer pooling is an example.

questions.prompt: Which are listed consequences of the Observer pattern?

options.text: Abstract coupling between Subject and Observer
Guaranteed compile-time type safety of updates

questions.explanation: Observer gives abstract coupling and broadcast support (pros) but risks unanticipated updates (con).

questions.prompt: A fluent interface uses extensive method chaining to improve readability, often forming a domain-specific language.
questions.explanation: Fluent interfaces rely on method chaining to read like prose and create a DSL-like API; Java Stream and Optional are examples.

questions.prompt: Which creational pattern is used when a complex object must be created through a complex, step-by-step interaction, with different variations possible?
questions.explanation: Builder is used when creating a complex object entails complex interaction and different variations of the target object might be produced (often with a fluent builder).

questions.prompt: What problem does the Abstract Factory pattern address?

options.text: A client should not know which variant of a family of related classes it is creating/using
An object needs exactly one instance
An existing interface is not the one the client expects and must be converted without modification
Behaviour must be added to objects dynamically

questions.explanation: Abstract Factory handles a family of related classes with different implementations so the client doesn't know which variant it is creating or using.

questions.prompt: Which are consequences of the Visitor pattern?

options.text: Adding new operations is very easy
It can visit class hierarchies and accumulate state
Adding new concrete elements is difficult
It strengthens encapsulation by keeping every operation inside the element classes themselves

questions.explanation: Visitor makes adding operations easy, can visit hierarchies and accumulate state, but makes adding new concrete elements difficult and breaks encapsulation.

questions.prompt: What characterizes duck typing in a dynamically typed language?

options.text: You just add a method to a class and can call it, with no compile-time type checking
You must declare interfaces and classes up front before you are ever allowed to call any method
All types are checked at compile time
Methods cannot be added after class definition

questions.explanation: With duck typing you simply add a method and call it — no interfaces or compile-time type checking, unlike strongly typed languages.

questions.prompt: Following the Java Bean convention, how are accessors for a property 'Prop' defined?

options.text: Getter getProp() and (optional) setter setProp(T value)
Only a public field named prop
A method prop() returning a map
An interface HasProp with no methods

questions.explanation: The Java Bean convention defines a getter getProp() and an optional setter setProp(T value) for a property Prop.

questions.prompt: Which pattern creates objects from a palette of similar classes to avoid a complex class hierarchy differentiated by minor parameters?
questions.explanation: Prototype creates objects from a palette of similar classes, avoiding a complex hierarchy whose classes differ only by minor parameters.

questions.prompt: Which pattern does this Java code from the slides implement?
questions.explanation: A private constructor plus a static getInstance() that lazily creates the single instance is the Singleton pattern. Source: SwD&A Design Patterns slides (Marco Torchiano) — 'Singleton class' example.

questions.prompt: Which design pattern is illustrated by Comparator in this slide example?
questions.explanation: Passing a java.util.Comparator to Arrays.sort embeds the comparison variation in a strategy object — the Strategy pattern. Source: SwD&A Design Patterns slides — 'Strategy example: Comparator'.

questions.prompt: Which pattern keeps the stable sort algorithm fixed while letting subclasses define compare()?
questions.explanation: Sorter defines the algorithm core and calls the abstract primitive compare(), which a subclass like StringSorter overrides — the Template Method pattern. Source: SwD&A Design Patterns slides — 'Example: Sorter / StringSorter'.

questions.prompt: Which idiom does this object-construction code from the slides demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Extensive method chaining that reads like prose to build a complex object is a fluent interface (DSL-like). Source: SwD&A Design Patterns slides — 'Fluent builder' example (Measure).

questions.prompt: Which patterns underlie the structure and evaluation of this expression tree from the slides?
questions.code:
Expression e = new Operation('*', new Value(6), new Operation('+', new Value(4), new Value(3)));
IO.println(e.formula() + " = " + e.eval());

options.text: Composite (operators and operands form a tree)
Singleton, to share one global evaluator instance across the whole expression tree

questions.explanation: The Abstract Syntax Tree uses Composite for operators/operands, and evaluation uses the Interpreter and Visitor patterns. Source: SwD&A Design Patterns slides — 'Abstract Syntax Tree / Expression Tree' example.

questions.prompt: In the GoF scope/purpose taxonomy, which pattern is classified as a CLASS-scoped behavioral pattern (relying on inheritance fixed at compile time) rather than an object-scoped one?
questions.explanation: Template Method (and Interpreter) are class-scoped behavioral patterns — they use inheritance, fixed statically. Strategy, Observer, and Mediator are object-scoped behavioral patterns that compose objects at run time.

questions.prompt: A class already in production exposes an interface a new client cannot use, and its source is unavailable. The integration must add no new behavior, only translate calls. Which is the MOST appropriate pattern, and why is Decorator wrong here?

options.text: Adapter — it converts the existing interface into the one the client expects
Decorator — it keeps the same interface but layers extra behavior onto the object at run time
Proxy — it keeps the same interface and interposes access control or lazy object creation
Facade — it fronts an entire subsystem of many classes behind one simplified higher-level interface

questions.explanation: Adapter converts one interface into another expected one without modifying the adaptee. Decorator preserves the component's interface and adds responsibilities; Proxy also keeps the same interface (controlling access); Facade simplifies a whole subsystem, not a single mismatched interface.

questions.prompt: Proxy, Decorator, and Adapter are all wrappers. Which statement correctly separates their intents?

options.text: Proxy keeps the interface to control access; Decorator keeps it to add responsibilities; Adapter converts it
Proxy adds responsibilities; Decorator converts the interface; Adapter controls access to the wrapped object
Adapter and Decorator both control access; Proxy is the one that converts between two interfaces
All three preserve the original interface and differ only in their run-time performance characteristics

questions.explanation: Intent distinguishes them: Proxy keeps the interface and controls access (remote/virtual/protection/smart reference); Decorator keeps the interface and adds responsibilities dynamically; Adapter changes the interface to the one the client expects.

questions.prompt: Strategy and State are structurally near-identical (an object delegating to a swappable companion). Which statements capture the REAL difference in intent?

options.text: Strategy varies an algorithm chosen by the client, and the strategies are usually unaware of one another
State varies behavior by the object's internal condition, and states often trigger transitions among themselves
Clients are typically aware of the strategies, whereas state transitions are normally kept internal
Both are class-scoped behavioral patterns that rely solely on inheritance and are bound statically at compile time

questions.explanation: Same structure, different intent: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms selected (often by the client, who is aware of them); State encapsulates condition-dependent behavior where states commonly drive transitions among themselves. They are not the same pattern.

questions.prompt: Abstract Factory and Factory Method both create products. What is the key structural distinction emphasized by GoF?

options.text: Abstract Factory builds related product families via composition; Factory Method makes one via subclassing
Factory Method builds families of related products via composition; Abstract Factory makes one via subclassing
Both patterns create their products purely through inheritance and never compose factory objects
Abstract Factory is a behavioral pattern, whereas Factory Method is a structural constructor wrapper

questions.explanation: Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating families of related objects and is typically realized through object composition; Factory Method defers instantiation of a single product to subclasses via inheritance (a class-scoped creational pattern).

questions.prompt: Per the slides, what are the trade-offs (consequences) of the Strategy pattern?

options.text: It avoids multiplying conditional statements and lets algorithms be organized into families
It supports run-time binding and gives clients a choice among interchangeable implementations
Clients must be aware of the different strategies, and there is some communication overhead
It removes the interface between algorithm and client, so no extra strategy objects are created

questions.explanation: Strategy consequences (from the slides): + avoids conditionals, organizes algorithm families, offers a choice of implementations and run-time binding; − clients must know the strategies, plus communication overhead and more objects. It still requires the strategy interface.

questions.prompt: A new operation must be added across an existing object structure of many fixed element classes, without polluting those classes with the operation. New element types are NOT expected. Which pattern fits, and what is its main downside?

options.text: Visitor — adding new operations is easy, but adding new concrete element types becomes hard
Strategy — operations stay easy to add, and brand-new element types are just as easy to add
Composite — elements are treated uniformly, but operations cannot accumulate any traversal state
Observer — operations are added in one place, but element updates always arrive unanticipated

questions.explanation: Visitor partitions operations away from the element classes, making new operations easy and able to accumulate state; its downside is that adding new concrete element types is hard and it can break encapsulation — acceptable here since element types are stable.

questions.prompt: The slides note that double-checked-free lazy Singleton 'getInstance()' can misbehave under concurrency. What is the underlying problem with the shown lazy implementation?

options.text: Two threads can both see instance == null and each build an instance, breaking uniqueness
The private constructor blocks every instantiation, so getInstance() can never return any object at all
A Java static field cannot hold an object reference, so the cached instance is always reset to null
getInstance() returns a fresh defensive copy on each call rather than the one shared instance

questions.explanation: The lazy 'if (instance == null) instance = new Singleton();' is not thread-safe: concurrent threads can both pass the null check and construct separate instances. Real implementations need synchronization, an eager static initializer, or a holder idiom.

questions.prompt: The slides contrast achieving the Observer relation via inheritance (extending Observable) versus composition (PropertyChangeSupport). Which are advantages of the COMPOSITION-based approach?

options.text: The subject need not extend a base class, so its single inheritance slot stays free for other use
Notification support is delegated to an embedded helper such as PropertyChangeSupport inside the subject
Listeners can subscribe to specific named properties rather than to the whole subject object
The subject inherits notifyObservers() from Observable and exposes those methods directly to clients

questions.explanation: Composition (PropertyChangeSupport) avoids consuming the subject's single base-class slot, delegates notification to an embedded object, and supports per-property listeners. Directly exposing inherited methods is a trait of the inheritance approach, not composition.

questions.prompt: Which pattern encapsulates a request as an object so it can be queued, logged, or undone, decoupling the invoker from the receiver?
questions.explanation: Command turns a request into an object, letting you parameterize, queue, log, or undo operations and decoupling sender from receiver. Memento captures/restores state; Mediator centralizes interactions; Chain of Responsibility passes a request along handlers.

questions.prompt: For the Flyweight pattern to reduce memory effectively, how must object state be handled?

options.text: Intrinsic, context-independent state lives in the shared flyweight; extrinsic state is passed in by the client
Both intrinsic and extrinsic state are duplicated inside every individual flyweight instance that is created
Extrinsic, context-dependent state lives in the flyweight; intrinsic state is supplied by the client each call
A flyweight must hold no state whatsoever, otherwise it can never be safely shared between contexts

questions.explanation: Flyweight shares intrinsic (context-independent) state inside the shared object and externalizes extrinsic (context-dependent) state to the client, so many fine-grained objects share one instance (e.g. Java Integer pooling, which has no extrinsic state).
